The central question is whether the same low-level computational circuits — specific patterns of weight interactions across MLP neurons — get recruited for mechanistically unrelated tasks, not because those tasks share semantics, but because superposition forces the network to pack multiple features into shared neuron directions, and co-activation patterns accidentally align across task boundaries. The key concepts are: superposition (the network represents more features than it has dimensions by encoding them as near-orthogonal directions in neuron activation space), circuits (subgraphs of weights and activations that implement a coherent function), and emergent reuse (a circuit shaped by one training objective turning out to partially implement another, with no explicit pressure to do so). The practical worry is that modular fine-tuning methods — LoRA, adapter layers, task vectors — assume circuits are somewhat separable, so updating weights for task B leaves task A's circuitry largely intact; but if circuits are entangled through superposition, a targeted fine-tune bleeds into seemingly unrelated capabilities in ways that aren't caught by standard eval suites. What a beginner misses is that the problem isn't just interference at the level of outputs (forgetting), but at the level of intermediate representations: a fine-tune can leave output benchmarks intact while silently corrupting the geometry of intermediate feature directions that other tasks depend on. The expert therefore worries less about catastrophic forgetting — which is visible — and more about subtle, task-specific degradation that only surfaces under distribution shift or compositional generalization tests where the corrupted geometry finally matters.

The cleanest signature is intervention asymmetry: if two tasks share a circuit because of genuine semantic overlap, then causally ablating that circuit (via activation patching or path patching, as in Wang et al.'s 2022 IOI work) should degrade both tasks proportionally, because both depend on the same sub-computation. But if the sharing is superposition-induced, ablating the circuit degrades the tasks unequally and in ways that depend on the direction of ablation, not just the magnitude — because the two tasks are using different linear subspaces of the same neurons, and a mean-ablation collapses both while a direction-specific ablation can dissociate them. A second signature is feature geometry under linear probing: genuinely shared sub-computations should produce task-relevant features that are aligned (small angles between probe weight vectors), whereas superposition-induced sharing produces features at large angles that merely co-habit the same neurons, detectable by the technique Elhage et al. A third, more demanding signature comes from scaling behavior: semantic sharing tends to be stable or grow with model scale as the shared concept becomes more robustly represented, while superposition-induced sharing is predicted to dissolve at sufficient scale because larger models can afford to unpack features into dedicated dimensions (the "phase transition" Elhage et al. describe around capacity thresholds). Practically, Conmy et al.'s ACDC circuit-discovery work (2023) gives you the tooling to check intervention asymmetry systematically, but almost no published circuit analysis has explicitly tested whether two discovered circuits are co-localized by geometry versus by function — that gap is itself telling about how underexplored this distinction remains.

The core failure mode is representational drift invalidating the SAE dictionary: the SAE learned a set of decoder directions that tile the base model's feature geometry, but fine-tuning rotates, scales, and merges those directions as weights update, so SAE features that were monosemantic at step 0 become misaligned garbage detectors by step 1000 — the SAE is now decomposing a space that no longer exists. This is more severe than ordinary distribution shift because it's not just that inputs changed; the linear subspace structure of the residual stream and MLP activations changed, meaning the SAE's encoder projections are measuring the wrong inner products entirely, and reconstruction loss on fine-tuning data will rise in ways that are hard to distinguish from "these are unusual inputs" versus "the geometry has moved." Concretely, Anthropic's sparse autoencoder work (Bricken et al., 2023) reports that SAE features are identified by their decoder directions in activation space; if fine-tuning rotates a layer's effective feature basis by even 15-20 degrees on average — plausible after a few hundred gradient steps with a standard LoRA rank-16 configuration — the cosine similarities between old SAE decoder vectors and new activation-space features drop enough that feature identity becomes unreliable. A second, subtler failure is feature splitting and merging: fine-tuning on a narrow task may cause two previously superposed features to disentangle (good) or two previously distinct features to collapse (bad), and the base SAE has no mechanism to detect either event because it has a fixed dictionary size and fixed decoder directions, so it silently misattributes activations to the nearest stale feature. The practical fix everyone reaches for — just retrain the SAE on fine-tuned model activations — is expensive and throws away the comparative baseline you need to actually measure what changed, suggesting the right architecture is an online SAE with a frozen base dictionary plus a small adaptive component that tracks drift, analogous to how continual learning methods maintain anchor points, but no such system has been demonstrated at the scale of current interpretability work.

Feature splitting helps modular fine-tuning safety if and only if the split is conservative — the two new dedicated directions span a subspace close to the original entangled direction, so downstream circuits that read from this layer via their key/query projections still receive approximately correct inputs — but hurts if the split involves a basis rotation that displaces unrelated features, which is the more likely outcome because gradient descent has no incentive to confine the new directions to the original subspace when rotating into unused capacity is lower loss. The diagnostic failure of SAE reconstruction loss as a signal is precise: disentanglement and corruption can both reduce reconstruction loss on fine-tuning task data because in both cases the SAE is now seeing more structured activations on that distribution, but corruption generates this structure by cannibalizing directions previously used by unrelated features, while genuine disentanglement carves new directions out of genuinely unused capacity — and reconstruction loss on the fine-tuning distribution cannot distinguish these because it never queries the displaced features. The distinguishing test requires held-out probing on features not targeted by fine-tuning: before and after, train linear probes for a battery of unrelated concepts (syntactic roles, factual entity types, arithmetic carries — the kind of features Geva et al. 2023 and Hernandez et al. 2023 identify in MLP layers) and check whether probe accuracy on those held-out features degrades; genuine disentanglement leaves them intact, corruption degrades them, and the SAE reconstruction loss signal is orthogonal to this distinction. A further signature is angular displacement of unrelated SAE features: after fine-tuning, compute cosine similarities between base-model SAE decoder vectors and the nearest neighbors in the fine-tuned model's activation PCA basis — beneficial splitting should show the targeted features moving while unrelated features stay anchored near their original directions, whereas corruption shows a broader angular displacement field affecting features far from the task-relevant cluster. The reason this matters practically is that LoRA's low-rank constraint (typically rank 8-64) bounds the dimensionality of the update but not its angular reach in the full activation space, meaning a rank-16 update can still rotate a 4096-dimensional layer's feature geometry substantially if the update directions happen to align with high-variance activation subspaces — a point that current LoRA safety arguments largely ignore.

A provable confinement result requires treating the SAE decoder matrix D ∈ ℝ^(d×k) (d = activation dimension, k = number of SAE features) as defining a "protected subspace" P = col(D_superposed), where D_superposed is the subcolumn corresponding to superposition-heavy features, and then constraining the LoRA update ΔW = BA to satisfy col(B) ⊥ P — enforced by projecting B's initialization and every gradient step onto P's orthogonal complement, which is a well-defined operation and costs one projection per step. The tightest bound you can derive is that if the superposition-heavy subspace has dimension s (estimated from SAE feature density, typically s ≈ 0.3–0.6 × d in MLP layers per Bricken et al.'s reported polysemanticity rates), then the maximum safe LoRA rank is (d - s), because any rank exceeding the codimension of P must by dimensionality arguments have at least one basis vector with nonzero projection onto P — meaning rank-16 is only provably safe if the protected subspace has dimension ≤ d - 16, which for d = 4096 and s ≈ 1500–2400 gives a comfortable margin, but for narrower bottleneck layers or heavily superposed attention heads the margin collapses. The practical problem is that this bound is static: it uses the SAE trained on the base model, but as we established, fine-tuning drifts the geometry, so the projection target P becomes stale mid-training and the confinement guarantee erodes exactly when it's most needed — the bound is tight at step 0 and increasingly loose thereafter. The closest existing work is GradOrth (gradient projection orthogonal to prior task subspace, used in continual learning by Farajtabar et al. 2020 and Saha et al. 2021's "GPM"), which projects gradient updates onto the null space of a stored feature matrix — the same operation, but computed from activation covariance rather than SAE decoder directions, meaning it protects high-variance directions rather than superposition-heavy ones, which are not the same thing and can be nearly orthogonal in adversarial cases. Yes, and the incompatibility is real and structured rather than a mere optimization inconvenience: if the fine-tuning objective requires gradient flow through directions in the protected subspace P, that means the task's required representational changes overlap with the base model's superposition-heavy directions, which can happen either because the task genuinely shares features with protected computations (semantic collision) or because the task is novel enough that the base model has no dedicated capacity for it and can only represent it by displacing existing superposed features (capacity collision) — and these two cases have different safety implications. You could formalize the diagnostic as a subspace alignment score: run a small number of fine-tuning steps without the orthogonality constraint, compute the distribution of gradient energy across the singular vectors of ΔW = BA, and measure what fraction lands inside P versus outside; a task that concentrates >50% of its gradient energy inside P is flagging either semantic or capacity collision, and the ratio gives you a continuous risk score before committing to a full fine-tune. This connects to the task arithmetic literature (Ilharco et al., 2023), where task vectors are shown to interfere when they have high cosine similarity in weight space — the diagnostic here is more precise because it operates in activation subspace rather than weight space, catching interference that task vector cosine similarity misses when two weight updates happen to produce similar weight deltas through mechanistically different paths. The capacity collision case is the more alarming one because it implies the base model is superposition-saturated for the target domain: the fine-tuning task cannot be learned without evicting existing features, meaning no constraint-based fine-tuning method can make it safe — the only remedies are growing the model (more dimensions) or accepting feature displacement and auditing which features are displaced, which requires exactly the held-out probing battery described earlier. Concretely, you could threshold the diagnostic: if subspace alignment score < 0.2, proceed with orthogonality-constrained LoRA; if 0.2–0.6, flag for human review and run held-out feature probing; if > 0.6, treat the fine-tune as fundamentally unsafe at current model scale and require either a larger base model or full retraining — a protocol that doesn't exist today but is derivable from tools already in hand.
